directly relevant English poetic treatments of the story see Faerie Queene III vi 29–49, and
Endymion ii 387–533. This fertility myth of a boy loved by a goddess, done to death by a
savage beast, and sleeping or waking with the seasonal life of Nature, parallels the fate of
Keats, a young poet loved by the Muse and killed by a Tory reviewer; whose body is reab-
sorbed into the vitality of Nature and whose spirit lives on with the enduring dead. This
narrative connects in Adonais with the theme of Moschus’s Lament for Bion, which artic-
ulates the classical formula of a shepherd-poet grieving for the loss of a fellow shepherd
and superior poet.
